summary: Medium-length security and compliance review focusing on incident response, business continuity and disaster recovery (BCDR), and SLA/escalation details. Redwood AE + SE explained standard offerings, discussed dedicated vs hosted options for residency, and agreed on next steps: share audit artifacts, run a tabletop DR exercise, and schedule a pilot failover test.

SLA and uptime guarantees, credits and measurement windows

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-03 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~45 mins | Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Jules (Redwood SE), Nina (Midland CISO), Ethan (Midland Cloud Ops), Priya (Legal), Carlos (Platform Eng)

[00:00] Avery: All right everyone thanks for joining on short notice, um this is Avery from Redwood, I'll kick off, quick intros?
[00:08] Nina: Hi I'm Nina Roberts, CISO at Midland. We have Ethan, Priya and Carlos from our side. Thanks for the invite.
[00:15] Samir: Hey Nina, thanks — I'm Samir, solutions engineer, I'll be walking through the BCDR and incident response bits.
[00:20] Jules: Jules here, platform SE, happy to dig into logs, KMS, any architecture questions.
[00:25] Ethan: Ethan Moore, Head of Cloud Ops. We're mainly concerned about RTO/RPO and how Redwood manages cross-region failover.
[00:32] Priya: Priya from Legal, I'll be listening for SLA language and breach/notification timelines.
[00:36] Carlos: Carlos, platform engineer, I'll be the hands-on for any test coordination.

[02:10] Samir: Cool, so the agenda — quick SOC/ISO artifact list, then incident classification (severity definitions), typical SLAs and uptime, BCDR mechanics including replication and failover, then escalation contacts. We'll leave time for Q/A.

[03:05] Nina: To start, our regulatory team needs RTO and RPO commitments per workload. For inference traffic we think of customer-facing flows as P1 — we need very short RTOs, ideally under 15 minutes for failover. Is that realistic?

[03:25] Samir: Yeah so typical Redwood hosted customers see multi-region failover, our standard targeted RTO for regional failover is around 10-20 minutes for service-level routing reconfiguration and model warmup, assuming models and artifacts are replicated. RPO depends on replication frequency — for stateless inference the user data isn’t stored, but internal state like KV caches can be rehydrated; we can put RPO targets as low as seconds with streaming replication or near-zero with synchronous replication on Dedicated/Private deployments. On hosted, asynchronous replication yields RPO in the order of minutes.

[04:12] Nina: When you say "synchronous on Dedicated/Private" — does that mean if we go Dedicated we can get near-zero RPO guaranteed?

[04:20] Jules: In Dedicated you control the cluster topology and we can set up synchronous replication across nodes in the pool; that reduces data loss for KV caches. For absolute guarantees we recommend Private deployment with customer-managed storage replication policies. We should capture which data matters: model binaries are replicated quickly — they are not the critical window. The critical is session state, audit logs, and any customer metadata.

[05:00] Ethan: Audit logs — retention and access. We need 7 years for certain audit trails, and privileged access should be exportable to our SIEM.

[05:12] Jules: We support configurable audit log retention policies; standard hosted retains sys-audit for 90 days by default but we offer longer retention as an add-on or via log export to your S3/Kafka. Exports can be delivered to your SIEM; logs include request IDs, model version, route, token usage, and account-level metadata. We'll share a sample log extract.

[06:05] Priya: On encryption: how is customer data encrypted at rest and in transit? KMS integration?

[06:12] Samir: In transit we use TLS 1.2+; at rest we encrypt model artifacts and logs. For hosted we use provider-managed KMS keys but can integrate with customer-managed keys (CMK) via KMS/HSM for Dedicated and Private. We'll include the KMS integration doc and key lifecycle information.

[07:30] Nina: SLA specifics — what's your uptime commitment and how are credits measured? Also what is the notification timeline for incidents impacting availability?

[07:40] Avery: Our baseline hosted SLA is 99.9% monthly uptime for enterprise customers, with credits calculated pro-rata based on downtime windows. For Dedicated contracts we can negotiate higher SLOs and tighter latency targets. For severity 1 incidents we aim for initial response within 15 minutes and continuous updates until remediation. Formal notice timelines and credit calculations are in the contract; we'll send the SLA matrix.

[09:02] Priya: By "initial response" you mean acknowledgement and assignment of an incident owner?

[09:06] Samir: Correct — initial triage and assignment to an on-call engineer, and then escalation to SE/AEC if needed.

[09:40] Carlos: Can you walk through the escalation chain? We need contacts and phone numbers for 24/7 pages for Sev1.

[09:50] Jules: Typically it goes: on-call SRE -> Redwood platform SE -> SE manager -> AE -> Redwood exec on-call. We provide a managed escalation list and support rotation in the engagement. For Dedicated/Private we can provide direct on-call numbers and integrate with your PagerDuty. We'll share a redacted escalation doc for contract.

[11:00] Ethan: For DR tests, what's the recommended cadence and what's a safe way to simulate failover without touching production?

[11:10] Samir: Tabletop annually and automated failover exercises quarterly in staging is common. We recommend a staging pilot where we simulate a regional outage: route a percentage of traffic to secondary region, validate model parity and latency, and then do a full cutover in a maintenance window. We'll help run the script and monitor post-failover metrics.

[12:55] Nina: I want concrete numbers for RTO/RPO. If we require RTO <= 15 minutes and RPO <= 1 minute for session metadata, are those achievable on hosted?

[13:10] Jules: On hosted, RTO 15 is on the tight side but achievable for stateless requests; for session metadata you'd want either synchronous replication or a small window of event streaming with near-real-time delivery. For absolute RPO <= 1 minute across the board, Dedicated or Private with configured replication is recommended. We'll provide a comparison table.

[15:00] Priya: Regarding notification and regulatory obligations — if there's an incident that impacts customer data, what's Redwood's obligation to notify customers and within what timeline?

[15:12] Avery: Contractually we notify customers within 72 hours for incidents that meet data breach definitions; for availability incidents we'll provide updates on the incident page and push notifications as configured. For banking customers we can negotiate faster notification clauses. We'll include our incident notification template.

[16:28] Ethan: A technical question — how do you handle model KV cache rehydration for warm caches after a failover? That affects perceived RTO/latency.

[16:36] Samir: Two approaches: 1) proactive replication of warmed caches for critical models; 2) fast rehydration pipelines that prefetch top n prefixes based on traffic heuristics. For very low-latency needs we combine sticky routing and cache mirroring. Rehydration adds a few seconds to minutes depending on model size and request patterns. We'll share metrics from a similar customer test.

[18:05] Nina: Do you maintain an audit trail of all config changes and failovers we can query for compliance reviews?

[18:12] Jules: Yes — all control-plane actions are logged with who/what/when and can be exported. We can also provide signed attestations for specific maintenance windows.

[19:00] Carlos: Network diagrams — we'll need peering/cidr and expected egress IP ranges for firewall rules during failover.

[19:10] Jules: We'll put together a network appendix showing endpoints, ports, and egress ranges, and a note on how the ranges may change during cross-region routing.

[21:30] Nina: One more compliance point — SOC 2 and ISO artifacts: can you provide scope and bridges for controls we already have to avoid duplicative audits?

[21:40] Avery: Yes. We'll share our SOC 2 Type II report, the ISO 27001 scope, and a control-mapping spreadsheet. We'll also include any open gaps and remediation timelines.

[23:05] Ethan: For escalation, what SLAs trigger an executive notification? Our policy requires exec-level awareness when customer-facing availability is impacted for more than 2 hours.

[23:15] Samir: We can bake that into the contract: if an incident is P1 and unresolved past 2 hours, exec-level escalation occurs automatically. We also support on-call paging for your SREs to be included.

[25:00] Priya: Legal will review indemnity and notification clauses; please provide the standard security appendix so we can redline.

[25:12] Avery: Will do — we'll attach the standard security appendix and highlight areas often redlined for banks.

[27:45] Carlos: On the tooling side, can we get read-only access to the audit logs via a service account so our SIEM ingestion is continuous?

[27:55] Jules: Yes, we can provision a read-only service principal for log export, with RBAC scopes limited to audit/log export. For hosted we provide a push export or an S3 pull model.

[29:10] Nina: For encryption keys, if we bring our own KMS, can we revoke keys and immediately revoke access? How does key rotation affect model availability?

[29:22] Samir: With customer-managed CMKs, key rotation is supported; revocation will block access until a new key is provided which would impact availability. We generally recommend a rotation policy that does not require emergency revocation, and we can coordinate key rotation windows. For Dedicated/Private deployments you have more immediate control.

[31:05] Ethan: Any recommended telemetry to monitor during a failover test?

[31:12] Samir: Yes — request success rate, tail latency (p95/p99), model inference error rate, token throughput, cache hit ratio, and queue length. We'll provide dashboards you can plug into.

[33:40] Nina: What about legal obligations for subpoenas or data requests — do you have a runbook for handling e-discovery?

[33:48] Priya: We need that documented; also logs access timestamps and chain-of-custody info.

[33:55] Jules: We have a legal and compliance playbook for subpoenas and e-discovery; logs include immutable timestamps and we can provide export with verifiable checksums for chain-of-custody. We'll include the playbook excerpt.

[36:00] Avery: Quick recap: Redwood to send SOC2/ISO artifacts, SLA matrix, KMS integration doc, sample audit log, escalation/contact list, and a proposed DR test plan. Midland to confirm RTO/RPO targets and provide possible DR windows.

[36:20] Nina: That matches our expectations. We'll review the artifacts and propose dates for the tabletop.

[37:05] Samir: One clarification — about RPO for session caches: if you require sub-minute RPO, we recommend Dedicated with synchronous replication; otherwise hosted with optimized streaming gives minute-scale RPO.

[38:30] Carlos: For the pilot failover, can Redwood simulate a regional blackhole rather than shutting services? That should be safer for our downstreams.

[38:40] Jules: Absolutely yes — we have traffic-shift scripts and can orchestrate a controlled routing failure to the secondary region without simulating infrastructure deletion. We'll run it in staging first.

[40:10] Priya: Two legal asks — can you confirm data residency (EU data stays in EU) and include it in the contract?

[40:18] Avery: We support region pinning and data residency controls; we'll include residency language and options for Private if you need strict physical controls.

[41:45] Nina: Anything else?

[41:50] Ethan: Just to confirm, next steps timing?

[41:56] Avery: We'll send the artifact bundle within 48 hours, set up the DR tabletop for week of Aug 10, and Samir/Jules will own runbook and pilot test planning.

[43:05] Priya: Thanks everyone, we'll loop Legal after we see the docs.

[43:12] Avery: Thanks, appreciate the time. We'll follow up with the package.

[44:30] Meeting ends.

Note: transcription contains minor filler words and occasional mis-attributions as typical of Fireflies exports. Some product names (e.g., "KV cache") may be transcribed inconsistently in places.
